title: Mainaka
hook: once, the story goes, mountains had wings, and one of them owes its wings to Hanuman's father
carry: a breath of wind long ago

segments.voice: Yesterday: Mainaka, the golden mountain who rose from the sea to offer rest, and Hanuman's hand on the summit as he said no, thank you. Your line was your welcome is as good as done. Did you decline something kindly? Today, why Mainaka cared. Day six hundred seven.

Sometimes a stranger is kind to you, and later you find out why. Your grandmother taught their mother to read. Your dad once pulled their car out of a ditch in the snow. The kindness wasn't really about you. It was a thank-you that had been waiting years for someone from your family to come along. When Mainaka rises from the sea, the Ocean has one reason to help. Mainaka, it turns out, has his own.
screen: `A STRANGER'S KINDNESS, EXPLAINED.` → `A THANK-YOU THAT WAITED YEARS.`

segments.voice: Mainaka tells Hanuman a story from the earliest age of the world. In those days, he says, the mountains had wings. They flew wherever they pleased, as fast as the wind, and the sages and the creatures below lived in fear that one would come down on them. So Indra, king of the gods, took up his thunderbolt and went after the mountains, cutting off their wings, one after another. When Indra came for Mainaka, the wind god Vayu swept him away, out of reach, and dropped him safely into the ocean, wings and all. Vayu, Mainaka reminds Hanuman, is your father. So I owe you. Helping you is how I pay your father back. Hold that next to yesterday. The Ocean helps because of Rama's ancestors. Mainaka helps because of Hanuman's father. Two old debts, from two different families, both coming due on the same crossing, over the same stretch of water. Valmiki is showing us a world where kindness doesn't disappear. It sinks below the surface, sometimes for ages, and then it rises when the right person passes. And there's a last turn. Indra, the very god who cut the mountains' wings, sees what Mainaka has done for Rama's messenger, and he's pleased. He grants Mainaka safety. The old enmity is set aside because of one good deed done for someone else's cause. Here the idea of karma, that actions bear fruit, is told not as a law but as a scene. A breath of wind long ago means a resting place today.
screen: `MOUNTAINS ONCE HAD WINGS.` · `INDRA CUTS THEM; VAYU SAVES MAINAKA.` · `TWO OLD DEBTS COME DUE.` · then, large: `INDRA GRANTS MAINAKA SAFETY.`

segments.voice: Settle and breathe. Think of a kindness someone in your family did long ago, one you've heard about but didn't witness: a grandparent, a parent, an aunt. Hold that story. Then think of a kindness you could do today that might not be repaid for years, or ever. You don't have to choose it now. Just let both rest together, the old one and the possible one, breathing in and out. The bell holds the time.
Mainaka. The winged mountain the wind god saved from Indra's thunderbolt, who repays that debt by rising to help Vayu's son, and is granted safety by Indra himself.
Your line: a breath of wind long ago. Today, ask an older relative about one kindness from your family's past, and listen for the whole story. Day six hundred seven.

howItsDone: The story of the winged mountains and Indra's thunderbolt is told in several Hindu texts, and in Sundara Kanda recitations Mainaka's speech is often read as a picture of gratitude carried across generations.

match.prompt: the winged mountain — tap the pairs.
pairs: carried Mainaka to safety in the sea
repays Vayu by helping his son

myth: in this story, mountains once had wings
they flew freely until Indra cut their wings with his thunderbolt.
Indra punishes Mainaka for helping Hanuman
Indra is pleased and grants Mainaka safety.
Mainaka helps only because the Ocean asked
he also owes Hanuman's father, Vayu, who saved his wings.

fork.setup: you're Indra. a mountain you once hunted has just helped Rama's messenger. what do you do?
options: finish the job and cut his wings.
grant him safety, pleased with his help.
fork.reveal: Indra is pleased with Mainaka's help to Hanuman and grants him safety, setting the old conflict aside.

original.note: Sanskrit vāyu, wind, and the wind god: Hanuman's father, who saved Mainaka.

trapdoor: what you thought: Mainaka is just a convenient rock in the sea.
what it means: he's repaying an ancient debt to Hanuman's father.
what a scholar hears: the winged mountains cut by Indra is an old myth found beyond the Ramayana; here it explains why Mainaka hides in the sea.

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Sundara Kanda 1 (Mainaka's story: the winged mountains, Indra, Vayu; Indra grants Mainaka safety)

notes: Mainaka's account (mountains with wings in an earlier age; Indra cutting them; Vayu carrying Mainaka into the ocean) and Indra granting Mainaka safety: confirm against Sundara 1.
The line about actions bearing fruit is a light gloss on karma; confirm the Keeper is comfortable with it.
The winged-mountain myth also appears in other texts (e.g., Vedic allusions to Indra and the mountains); confirm the trapdoor wording.
